title: MaxDiff Analysis of MSBA Class Preferences
text:
Hello World! The MSBA program is unique in that it allows students to select a number of electives to support their technical classes. I was curious to see how students rank these electives against one another (and the core classes). This is harder than it sounds; preferences are a tricky thing to assign a numeric value to. Some people never give out a ‘10/10’, while others give full points to every class. Maybe they suspect the surveys aren’t as anonymous as they claim to be… who knows!
MaxDiff (also called Best-Worst Scaling) sidesteps this problem by forcing trade-offs. On each screen of the survey, respondents see a small subset of items — four classes in this case — and identify the most-preferred and the least-preferred. A simple: “of these four, which would you most want to take, and which least?” People are very good at this kind of relative judgment. It’s like asking “chocolate ice cream, or vanilla?” across many screens, with the subsets shuffled (chocolate ice cream, vs vanilla, vs caramel, vs rocky-road-max-diabetes-cotton-candy-mint…), generates enough comparisons to recover a full preference ranking.
This analysis uses MaxDiff data collected from our cohort. One consideration is that the class the survey was distributed in is included in the analysis. The ten items are the ten core + elective MSBA courses at UCSD Rady. The goal is to estimate how strongly students prefer each course, using three methods of increasing sophistication:

Counts analysis — the simplest possible summary: for each class, percent of times chosen best minus percent chosen worst.
Multinomial Logit (MNL) via Maximum Likelihood — models the choice process explicitly and returns point estimates with standard errors.
MNL via Bayesian estimation (Metropolis-Hastings MCMC) — same model, but returns a full posterior distribution, making uncertainty about derived quantities (like preference shares) easy to quantify.

All three methods should broadly agree on the ranking. The interesting action is at the edges: where they disagree, and what each adds over the simpler approach before it.

title: MaxDiff Analysis of MSBA Class Preferences
text:
Counts Analysis
The simplest way to summarize MaxDiff data is to ignore the model entirely and just count. For each item, compute:

% best: fraction of times it was picked best out of all the times it was shown
% worst: fraction of times it was picked worst out of all the times it was shown
Score: % best − % worst

A score near +1 means the class is almost always chosen as the top pick when it appears; near −1 means it’s almost always the least preferred. Near zero means it’s either genuinely middling, or it’s polarizing — loved by some, disliked by others.

# Aggregate counts per item
counts = df4.groupby('Item').agg(
    shown=('Response', 'count'),
    n_best=('Response', lambda x: (x == 1).sum()),
    n_worst=('Response', lambda x: (x == -1).sum())
).reset_index()

counts['pct_best']  = counts['n_best']  / counts['shown']
counts['pct_worst'] = counts['n_worst'] / counts['shown']
counts['score']     = counts['pct_best'] - counts['pct_worst']
counts = counts.merge(labels[['Item','label','short']], on='Item')
counts = counts.sort_values('score', ascending=False).reset_index(drop=True)
counts['rank'] = range(1, 11)

display_cols = ['rank','short','shown','n_best','n_worst',
                'pct_best','pct_worst','score']

What we see: SQL and Customer Analytics sit clearly at the top — students reliably pick them best and avoid picking them worst. At the other end, Capstone Project and Marketing/Finance/Operations score negatively, meaning they’re more often the least preferred choice when shown. BI Systems and Analytics Consulting occupy a muddled middle ground where confidence intervals overlap zero. The bootstrap CIs confirm that the top and bottom positions are genuinely stable; the middle of the ranking is noisier.

title: MaxDiff Analysis of MSBA Class Preferences
section: From MaxDiff Data to MNL Choices
text:
From MaxDiff Data to MNL Choices
To go beyond counts, we need a model. The multinomial logit (MNL) assigns each class \(j\) a utility parameter \(\beta_j\). When a respondent sees four classes \(\{a, b, c, d\}\), the probability they pick \(b\) as best is the familiar softmax:
\[
P(\text{best} = b) = \frac{\exp(\beta_b)}{\exp(\beta_a) + \exp(\beta_b) + \exp(\beta_c) + \exp(\beta_d)}
\]
After the best pick, the worst pick comes from the three remaining items — but now with negated utilities, because choosing the least preferred is like choosing the best on an inverted scale:
\[
P(\text{worst} = c \mid \text{best} = b) = \frac{\exp(-\beta_c)}{\exp(-\beta_a) + \exp(-\beta_c) + \exp(-\beta_d)}
\]
So each task screen gives us two MNL observations: one for the best pick from 4, and one for the worst pick from the remaining 3.
One important wrinkle: the softmax only cares about differences in \(\beta\), not their absolute values. If you add a constant to every \(\beta\), all the choice probabilities stay exactly the same. This means the model isn’t identified unless we fix a reference. I set \(\beta_1 = 0\) (AI Math & Analytics as the anchor) and estimate the remaining nine.

# Reshape data into one row per task
# Each row: respondent, task, list of 4 items, which was best, which was worst
tasks = []
for (rid, task_id), grp in df4.groupby(['Record ID', 'Task']):
    items = grp['Item'].tolist()
    best_item  = grp.loc[grp['Response'] ==  1, 'Item'].iloc[0]
    worst_item = grp.loc[grp['Response'] == -1, 'Item'].iloc[0]
    tasks.append({
        'resp': rid,
        'task': task_id,
        'items': items,
        'best': best_item,
        'worst': worst_item
    })

task_df = pd.DataFrame(tasks)
print(f"Total tasks: {len(task_df)}")
print(task_df.head(5).to_string(index=False))

title: MaxDiff Analysis of MSBA Class Preferences
text:
MNL via Maximum Likelihood
The log-likelihood sums over all tasks. For each task, it adds the log-probability of the observed best pick and the log-probability of the observed worst pick (from remaining items with flipped utilities):
\[
\ell(\boldsymbol{\beta}) = \sum_{\text{tasks}} \left[
  \beta_{j^*_b} - \log \sum_{j \in \text{shown}} \exp(\beta_j)
  - \beta_{j^*_w} - \log \sum_{j \in \text{shown} \setminus \{j^*_b\}} \exp(-\beta_j)
\right]
\]

def get_beta_full(beta9):
    """Expand 9-vector to 10-vector with beta[0] = 0 (item 1 is reference)."""
    return np.concatenate([[0.0], beta9])

def log_likelihood(beta9):
    beta = get_beta_full(beta9)
    ll = 0.0
    for _, row in task_df.iterrows():
        items = row['items']   # list of 4 item numbers (1-indexed)
        best  = row['best']
        worst = row['worst']
        
        # Item indices into beta (item j -> beta[j-1])
        idx   = [i - 1 for i in items]
        utils = beta[idx]
        
        # Log-prob of best pick (softmax denominator = all 4)
        ll += utils[items.index(best)] - np.log(np.sum(np.exp(utils)))
        
        # Log-prob of worst pick from remaining 3 (with negated utilities)
        remaining = [i for i in items if i != best]
        r_idx     = [i - 1 for i in remaining]
        r_utils   = -beta[r_idx]  # negate for "worst" direction
        ll += r_utils[remaining.index(worst)] - np.log(np.sum(np.exp(r_utils)))
    
    return ll

# Maximize (minimize the negative log-likelihood)
# L-BFGS-B handles this scale of problem cleanly and gives reliable convergence
result = minimize(
    fun=lambda b: -log_likelihood(b),
    x0=np.zeros(9),
    method='L-BFGS-B',
    options={'maxiter': 5000, 'ftol': 1e-12, 'gtol': 1e-8}
)

beta_hat = get_beta_full(result.x)
print(f"Optimization converged: {result.success}")
print(f"Log-likelihood at MLE:  {-result.fun:.2f}")

Optimization converged: True
Log-likelihood at MLE:  -1572.73



# Standard errors from numerical Hessian of the log-likelihood
# L-BFGS-B doesn't return an exact Hessian, so we compute it numerically
from scipy.optimize import approx_fprime

def hessian_numerical(f, x, eps=1e-4):
    """Numerical Hessian via finite differences."""
    n = len(x)
    H = np.zeros((n, n))
    for i in range(n):
        def grad_i(x_):
            return approx_fprime(x_, f, eps)[i]
        H[i] = approx_fprime(x, grad_i, eps)
    return H

# Hessian of the negative log-likelihood at the MLE
H = hessian_numerical(lambda b: -log_likelihood(b), result.x, eps=1e-4)
se9 = np.sqrt(np.diag(np.linalg.inv(H)))
se_full = np.concatenate([[np.nan], se9])  # item 1 is fixed, no SE

# Shares of preference
shares = np.exp(beta_hat) / np.sum(np.exp(beta_hat))

# Build results table
mle_df = pd.DataFrame({
    'Item':   range(1, 11),
    'beta':   beta_hat,
    'se':     se_full,
    'share':  shares
}).merge(labels[['Item','short']], on='Item')
mle_df = mle_df.sort_values('share', ascending=False).reset_index(drop=True)
mle_df['rank'] = range(1, 11)

fmt_mle = mle_df[['rank','short','beta','se','share']].copy()

fmt_mle['share'] = fmt_mle['share'].map('{:.3f}'.format)
fmt_mle.columns = ['Rank','Class','β̂','SE(β̂)','Share']
print(fmt_mle.to_string(index=False))

mle_sorted = mle_df.copy()
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 6))
colors = ['#D4537E' if s > 0.1 else '#8B8FA8' for s in mle_sorted['share']]

Comparing MLE to counts: The top two (SQL, Customer Analytics) and the bottom two (Capstone, Mktg/Fin/Ops) are identical across both methods. The middle shuffles slightly. MLE tends to compress the middle more than counts because it borrows information from all the “not chosen” events — every time a class was shown and not picked tells us something, and the model uses that signal. The counts method treats not-best and not-worst as pure abstentions.

title: MaxDiff Analysis of MSBA Class Preferences
text:
MNL via Bayesian Estimation
Now we fit the same MNL model, but instead of a point estimate we want the full posterior distribution over \(\boldsymbol{\beta}\). The posterior is:
\[
\pi(\boldsymbol{\beta} \mid \boldsymbol{y}) \propto L(\boldsymbol{\beta}) \cdot \pi(\boldsymbol{\beta})
\]
I use a weakly informative prior: \(\boldsymbol{\beta} \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\; 10 \cdot I)\). With a standard deviation of about 3.2 on each \(\beta\), this prior is diffuse enough not to pull the estimates away from the likelihood, but informative enough to rule out absurdly large utilities.
To sample the posterior I use a random-walk Metropolis-Hastings algorithm. The sampler proposes a small random step from the current \(\boldsymbol{\beta}\), computes the log-posterior at the proposal, and accepts or rejects based on the Metropolis ratio. Over many iterations, the accepted draws trace out the posterior.

def log_prior(beta9):
    return np.sum(-0.5 * beta9**2 / 10)  # N(0, 10) on each of 9 betas

def log_posterior(beta9):
    return log_likelihood(beta9) + log_prior(beta9)

def metropolis_hastings(beta0, n_iter, step, seed=123):
    rng_mh = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    K = len(beta0)
    draws = np.zeros((n_iter, K))
    beta = beta0.copy()
    lp = log_posterior(beta)
    accepted = 0
    
    for t in range(n_iter):
        # Propose a step
        proposal = beta + rng_mh.normal(0, step, size=K)
        lp_prop = log_posterior(proposal)
        
        # Accept or reject
        if np.log(rng_mh.uniform()) < lp_prop - lp:
            beta = proposal
            lp = lp_prop
            accepted += 1
        
        draws[t] = beta
    
    return draws, accepted / n_iter


# Tune the step size to get ~25-40% acceptance
# Start from the MLE solution for faster burn-in
beta_start = result.x.copy()

# Quick tuning runs (2000 iterations each)
for step_try in [0.01, 0.05, 0.07, 0.08, 0.10]:
    _, rate = metropolis_hastings(beta_start, 2000, step_try, seed=99)
    print(f"  step = {step_try:.2f}  ->  acceptance = {rate:.1%}")

# Posterior summaries
# Full beta draws (10 items, with item 1 = 0 pinned)
draws_full = np.hstack([np.zeros((len(draws), 1)), draws])

post_mean = draws_full.mean(axis=0)
post_lo   = np.percentile(draws_full, 2.5, axis=0)
post_hi   = np.percentile(draws_full, 97.5, axis=0)

# Posterior shares: compute share for every draw, then take mean
# shape: (n_draws, 10)
exp_draws = np.exp(draws_full)

What the three methods agree on: SQL and Customer Analytics are clearly the most preferred courses — they top the ranking in all three methods, and by a meaningful margin. At the bottom, Capstone Project and Marketing/Finance/Operations sit last (or near-last) consistently. The top and bottom of any preference ranking tend to be the most robust findings: extreme preferences generate a lot of signal.
Where they disagree: The middle four or five courses shuffle depending on the method. Counts scores for courses like Business Analytics and BI Systems are close to zero, and small differences in the denominator (how many times each was shown) can flip their relative order. MLE and Bayes are more stable here because they use all the choice information — not just the best and worst picks, but the implicit information in being shown and not chosen.
What MNL adds over counts: Counts treats “shown and not chosen” as uninformative. MNL doesn’t. When item A is shown alongside a very strong item B and doesn’t get picked, that’s less damning than not getting picked against a weak field. The likelihood function captures this — it uses the full softmax denominator, which reflects the quality of the competition in each task.
What Bayes adds over MLE: The MLE gives a single point estimate and standard errors. The Bayesian approach gives a full posterior distribution. This matters when you want uncertainty quantification on derived quantities. Getting a credible interval on the share of preference for “SQL” is trivial with MCMC — just push each draw through the softmax and take the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles. From MLE, you’d need the delta method, which involves a Jacobian. Bayes also scales naturally to hierarchical extensions, where you estimate individual-level preferences instead of one pooled model.

title: MaxDiff Analysis of MSBA Class Preferences
text:
Discussion
If I had to summarize this analysis for a student choosing their MSBA electives or an academic advisor designing the program: SQL and Customer Analytics are genuinely beloved, and Capstone and the combined Mktg/Fin/Ops course are reliably least preferred. Those findings are robust to choice of method. The middle of the ranking — Business Analytics, BI Systems, AI Math & Analytics — is less settled, and the uncertainty in that region is real.
Methodologically, the three approaches exist on a spectrum of complexity and payoff:

Counts is the right tool when you need a quick, defensible number for a dashboard or stakeholder update. It requires no modeling assumptions, is easy to explain, and is hard to game or misinterpret.
MLE MNL is the right tool when you need rigor: you want a formal statistical model, point estimates with standard errors, and the ability to say something about the choice process rather than just the aggregate tallies.
Bayesian MNL is the right tool when you want to do something more: quantify uncertainty on nonlinear derived quantities (like shares or market simulations), extend the model hierarchically to estimate individual preferences, or formally incorporate prior information from a previous study.

A few caveats worth flagging: this is a self-selected sample of students who are still in the program. People who dropped out or transferred aren’t in this data. Students in different quarters have experienced different subsets of these courses, which affects their priors going in. Additionally, the program has a big range of techincal students, vs soft-skill-oriented students. And the framing of the survey — “which course would you prefer?” — likely mixes “which course did I personally enjoy” with “which course do I think is most valuable,” which aren’t the same thing.
One could also extend this to a hierarchical MNL model to estimate individual-level utilities. That is a task for someone who has finished their capstone project! Possibly myself in circa 10 weeks.

title: Poisson Regression and Maximum Likelihood Estimation
text:
Blueprinty makes software that helps engineering firms prepare and submit patent applications. Their marketing team wants to make a compelling claim: firms that use Blueprinty win more patents. If true, this could be a powerful selling point. The problem? How do we prove this…
The ideal study would be a randomized experiment, where some firms use the software, and some don’t. We’d compare the outcomes of both. But that’s not what Blueprinty has. Instead, they’ve collected observational data on 1,500 mature engineering firms, recording the number of patents each firm was awarded over the last five years, each firm’s region, its age since incorporation, and whether it’s a Blueprinty customer (!).
With a key complication… Blueprinty’s customers self-selected into using the product. There was no randomization. That means any raw difference in patent counts between customers and non-customers could reflect the fact that, say, customers tend to be in regions with more patent activity, or that they’re newer firms with more to prove. Before we can say anything credible about the software’s effect, we need to account for those confounders. That’s what poisson regression is going to help with.

Exploring the Data



Patent count distributions for customers vs. non-customers. Vertical dashed lines mark group means.


Blueprinty customers average 4.13 patents over the five-year window, compared to 3.47 for non-customers; a gap of ~ 0.66 patents. Both distributions are right-skewed and peak around 3–4 patents. But the raw mean difference doesn’t tell us whether the software caused the gap (remember those confounds?). To figure that out, we first need to look at who the customers actually are.

Are customers systematically different?



Left: age distributions largely overlap. Right: Northeast is dramatically over-represented among Blueprinty customers.


Two things should stand out to you here. First, age distributions for customers and non-customers look very similar: means of 26.9 vs. 26.1 years. So, age probably isn’t driving the raw patent gap. Second, region is a major confounder. Nearly 68% of Blueprinty customers are in the Northeast, versus only 27% of non-customers. If Northeastern firms tend to file more patents regardless of software (perhaps because they’re clustered near research universities, or tech corridors), that alone could explain part of the raw difference. Our analysis should control for the region.

title: Poisson Regression and Maximum Likelihood Estimation
section: A Simple Poisson Model via Maximum Likelihood
text:
A Simple Poisson Model via Maximum Likelihood
Warning: The Math Section
Patent counts are non-negative integers; they can’t be negative, and they’re discrete. A Normal distribution is a poor fit for this kind of outcome - it assigns probability to negative values, and allows for fractional counts. The Poisson distribution is the next natural starting point for count data. It’s parameterized by a single rate \(\lambda > 0\), which equals both the mean and variance of the distribution.

Deriving the likelihood
If each firm’s patent count \(Y_i\) is an independent draw from \(\text{Poisson}(\lambda)\), the probability of observing a single count is:
\[
f(Y_i \mid \lambda) = \frac{e^{-\lambda} \lambda^{Y_i}}{Y_i!}
\]
The joint likelihood across all \(n = 1{,}500\) firms is the product of individual probabilities (by independence):
\[
L(\lambda \mid \mathbf{Y}) = \prod_{i=1}^{n} \frac{e^{-\lambda} \lambda^{Y_i}}{Y_i!}
\]
Taking the log converts the product into a sum and makes the math tractable:
\[
\ell(\lambda) = \log L(\lambda \mid \mathbf{Y}) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \left[ -\lambda + Y_i \log\lambda - \log(Y_i!) \right]
\]
Simplifying (the \(\log(Y_i!)\) terms are constants with respect to \(\lambda\)):
\[
\ell(\lambda) = -n\lambda + \left(\sum_{i=1}^{n} Y_i\right) \log\lambda - \text{const}
\]
To find the MLE analytically, take the derivative and set it to zero:
\[
\frac{d\ell}{d\lambda} = -n + \frac{\sum Y_i}{\lambda} = 0 \implies \hat\lambda_{\text{MLE}} = \bar{Y}
\]
This makes intuitive sense — the MLE for the Poisson rate is just the sample mean.


Visualizing the log-likelihood

Y = df["patents"].values

def poisson_loglik(lam, Y):
    """Log-likelihood for Y ~ Poisson(lambda), omitting the constant log(Y!) term."""
    return np.sum(-lam + Y * np.log(lam))

lambdas = np.linspace(0.5, 8, 400)
ll_vals = [poisson_loglik(l, Y) for l in lambdas]




The log-likelihood peaks exactly at \(\bar{Y} = 3.685\), confirming the analytic result.


The curve is concave and unimodal — there’s a single maximum. The peak falls at \(\hat\lambda = \bar{Y} = 3.685\), confirming the analytic derivation. This is the value of \(\lambda\) most consistent with the data.


Numerical confirmation

result_simple = optimize.minimize_scalar(
    lambda lam: -poisson_loglik(lam, Y),
    bounds=(0.1, 20),
    method="bounded"
)
lambda_mle = result_simple.x



Numerical MLE (scipy):  3.684667
Sample mean (analytic): 3.684667


The numerical optimizer agrees with \(\bar{Y}\) to six decimal places, as expected.

title: Poisson Regression and Maximum Likelihood Estimation
text:
Poisson Regression
The simple model above assumes every firm shares the same patent rate \(\lambda\) — clearly too restrictive. Older firms may have different rates than newer ones; firms in the Northeast may differ from those in the South. Poisson regression relaxes this by letting \(\lambda\) vary across firms as a function of their characteristics:
\[
Y_i \sim \text{Poisson}(\lambda_i), \qquad \lambda_i = \exp(X_i'\beta)
\]
We use \(\exp(\cdot)\) as the link function because \(\lambda_i\) must be strictly positive, but \(X_i'\beta\) can be any real number. The exponential maps the linear predictor onto the positive real line.

Building the covariate matrix
The design matrix \(X\) includes: - An intercept column of ones - Firm age and age squared — the relationship between age and patenting is likely nonlinear (young firms ramp up, very old ones may stagnate), so including the quadratic term lets the model capture that curvature - Region dummies for Northeast, Northwest, South, and Southwest, with Midwest as the omitted baseline — we must drop one region to avoid perfect collinearity with the intercept - The customer indicator — the variable we care most about

region_dummies = pd.get_dummies(df["region"], drop_first=True, prefix="region").astype(float)

X = pd.concat([
    pd.Series(1.0, index=df.index, name="const"),
    df[["age", "iscustomer"]].astype(float),
    region_dummies
], axis=1)
X.insert(2, "age_sq", (df["age"] ** 2).astype(float))

Y_reg = df["patents"].astype(float)



Log-likelihood for Poisson regression
The log-likelihood extends naturally from the simple case — we just replace the scalar \(\lambda\) with the vector \(\lambda_i = \exp(X_i'\beta)\):

def poisson_reg_loglik(beta, Y, X):
    Xb  = np.clip(X.values @ beta, -50, 50)   # clip for numerical stability
    lam = np.exp(Xb)
    return np.sum(Y * np.log(lam + 1e-300) - lam)



Finding the MLE with scipy.optimize

beta_init = np.zeros(X.shape[1])

res = optimize.minimize(
    lambda b: -poisson_reg_loglik(b, Y_reg, X),
    beta_init,
    method="BFGS",
    options={"maxiter": 5000}
)

beta_optim = res.x



Optimization converged: False
Coefficients: {'const': -0.50999, 'age': 0.14871, 'age_sq': -0.00297, 'iscustomer': 0.20761, 'region_Northeast': 0.02916, 'region_Northwest': -0.01758, 'region_South': 0.05657, 'region_Southwest': 0.05057}




Checking against statsmodels

glm_result = glm_model.fit()

Region: Northeast      0.0292     0.0436        0.67   0.504

The scipy.optimize coefficients and statsmodels GLM coefficients agree closely — any small differences arise from the numerical approximation of the Hessian in BFGS versus the analytically computed Fisher information matrix used by the GLM. For all subsequent inference we use the GLM estimates, which are more precise.



Coefficient estimates with 95% confidence intervals. Pink markers are statistically significant at the 5% level.




Interpreting the coefficients
Because the model is log-linear, coefficients are interpreted as multiplicative effects on the expected patent count (i.e., \(e^\beta\) gives a rate ratio):

Age has a positive coefficient (0.149), and age² has a negative one (−0.003), indicating an inverted-U relationship — patent activity rises with firm age but eventually plateaus or declines. This is the classic “life cycle” pattern in innovation.
Region coefficients are small and not statistically significant, suggesting that after controlling for age and customer status, regional differences in patent rates are modest.
The customer coefficient (0.208) is positive and highly significant (\(p < 0.001\)). In isolation it would imply that customers have \(e^{0.208} \approx 1.23\times\) the patent rate of otherwise identical non-customers — a 23% multiplicative lift. But because the model is multiplicative, converting this to an interpretable number of additional patents requires a counterfactual calculation.

title: Poisson Regression and Maximum Likelihood Estimation
text:
The Effect of Blueprinty’s Software
A coefficient alone doesn’t tell us how many more patents a firm would expect to win if it became a Blueprinty customer. To get that, we construct two counterfactual worlds:

X0 = X.copy(); X0["iscustomer"] = 0.0   # everyone is a non-customer
X1 = X.copy(); X1["iscustomer"] = 1.0   # everyone is a customer

yhat_0 = np.exp(X0.values @ glm_result.params.values)
yhat_1 = np.exp(X1.values @ glm_result.params.values)

ate = (yhat_1 - yhat_0).mean()
print(f"Average treatment effect: {ate:.4f} additional patents")

Average treatment effect: 0.7928 additional patents


Holding firm age and region fixed at their observed values and simply switching customer status, the model predicts that Blueprinty customers win on average ~0.79 more patents over the five-year window.



The predicted effect of Blueprinty’s software across all 1,500 firms. Individual effects vary because \(\lambda_i\) depends on each firm’s age and region.


The distribution of individual effects is narrow — nearly all firms are predicted to gain somewhere between 0.75 and 0.85 patents — because the Poisson regression model is fairly smooth. Effects are slightly larger for firms with higher baseline patent rates (older firms in the Northeast), since the customer coefficient acts multiplicatively.

What can we actually conclude?
The analysis is consistent with Blueprinty’s marketing claim: firms using the software are associated with meaningfully more approved patents, even after controlling for age and regional location. That’s a stronger statement than a raw mean comparison.
But this is an observational study, not a randomized experiment. We’ve controlled for age and region, but there may be other differences between customers and non-customers that we can’t measure — perhaps customers have better internal R&D processes, or more sophisticated legal teams, or simply have more to gain from patent protection and therefore invest more broadly in the application process. Any of those unobserved factors could be driving part or all of the estimated effect. The right tool for resolving that ambiguity would be a randomized controlled trial or a natural experiment.
For now, the data give Blueprinty’s marketing team a defensible, methodologically grounded argument — one that holds up to basic confounder adjustment. The honest version of the claim: firms using Blueprinty’s software are associated with approximately 0.79 more approved patents over five years, controlling for firm age and region.

  The Problem with Propensity Targeting

  Most marketing models ask: who is most likely to convert? That sounds right — but it's the wrong question. Targeting high-propensity users wastes budget on two groups: people who would have converted anyway (Sure Things), and people who actually respond negatively to outreach (Sleeping Dogs).

  Uplift modeling reframes the question as: for whom does the treatment cause conversion? This is a causal inference problem. The goal is to estimate the individual treatment effect — the difference in conversion probability between a user who receives the action and the same user in a counterfactual world where they don't.

  
    Maximizing conversion rate is not the same as maximizing profit.
  

  Because we can never observe both outcomes for the same person, uplift models are trained on randomized control trial data — where treatment assignment is independent of user characteristics — and the target is the estimated difference in outcomes, not the outcome itself.

  

  
  The Four Customer Segments

  
    
      Persuadables
      Convert if treated, don't if untreated. These are the only users where the treatment creates genuine incremental value.
      Target
    
    
      Sure Things
      Convert regardless of treatment. Targeting them wastes spend without any lift in outcome.
      Skip
    
    
      Lost Causes
      Won't convert regardless. No treatment will change this — budget is better spent elsewhere.
      Skip
    
    
      Sleeping Dogs
      Less likely to convert if treated. Outreach actively hurts conversion — these users must be excluded.
      Avoid

Approach

Logistic Regression

title: A/B Testing a Call to Action
text:
My website has a landing page where visitors can sign up for a newsletter. A natural question is: does the wording of the sign-up prompt actually matter? To find out, I tested two versions of the call to action (CTA):

CTA A: “Sign up for our newsletter here!”
CTA B: “Stay up to date by signing up!”

To evaluate which performs better, I ran an A/B test — visitors are randomly assigned to see one of the two CTAs, and I compare sign-up rates between the two groups. Random assignment is the key: it ensures that any difference in sign-up rates is attributable to the CTA language itself, not to some other difference between the groups.

title: A/B Testing a Call to Action
text:
My website has a landing page where visitors can sign up for a newsletter. A natural question is: does the wording of the sign-up prompt actually matter? To find out, I tested two versions of the call to action (CTA):

CTA A: “Sign up for our newsletter here!”
CTA B: “Stay up to date by signing up!”

To evaluate which performs better, I ran an A/B test — visitors are randomly assigned to see one of the two CTAs, and I compare sign-up rates between the two groups. Random assignment is the key: it ensures that any difference in sign-up rates is attributable to the CTA language itself, not to some other difference between the groups.

title: A/B Testing a Call to Action
section: The A/B Test as a Statistical Problem
text:
The A/B Test as a Statistical Problem
Each visitor either signs up or doesn’t — a binary outcome. We model each visitor’s outcome as a draw from a Bernoulli distribution with parameter \(\pi\), the probability of signing up. Since CTA language may influence that probability, we allow it to differ across groups:

Visitors who see CTA A have sign-up probability \(\pi_A\)
Visitors who see CTA B have sign-up probability \(\pi_B\)

The quantity we care about is the true difference in sign-up rates:
\[\theta = \pi_A - \pi_B\]
We estimate this with the difference in sample proportions:
\[\hat{\theta} = \bar{X}_A - \bar{X}_B\]
Since each observation is 0 or 1, the sample mean is simply the fraction of visitors who signed up — so \(\bar{X}_A = \hat{\pi}_A\) and \(\bar{X}_B = \hat{\pi}_B\).

title: A/B Testing a Call to Action
text:
Simulating Data
In a real experiment, \(\pi_A\) and \(\pi_B\) are unknown. But for this exercise, we set them ourselves so we can study how our estimator behaves when we know the truth. Suppose \(\pi_A = 0.22\) and \(\pi_B = 0.18\), making the true difference \(\theta = 0.04\) — CTA A is slightly better.

import numpy as np
np.random.seed(42)

pi_A = 0.22
pi_B = 0.18
n = 1000

draws_A = np.random.binomial(1, pi_A, n)
draws_B = np.random.binomial(1, pi_B, n)

theta_hat = draws_A.mean() - draws_B.mean()
print(f"Estimated θ: {theta_hat:.4f}  (True θ: 0.04)")

Estimated θ: 0.0380  (True θ: 0.04)

title: A/B Testing a Call to Action
text:
The Law of Large Numbers
The Law of Large Numbers (LLN) tells us that as sample size grows, the sample mean converges to the population mean. This is what gives us confidence that \(\hat{\theta} = \bar{X}_A - \bar{X}_B\) will be close to the true \(\theta\) when the sample is large enough — it’s not just luck, it’s a theorem.
To see this in action, I compute the element-wise differences between the CTA A and CTA B draws, then plot the running (cumulative) average of those differences as sample size grows.

diffs = draws_A - draws_B
cumulative_avg = np.cumsum(diffs) / np.arange(1, n + 1)










With only a handful of observations, the running average is noisy and swings around. But as sample size grows, it settles toward the true difference of 0.04. This is the LLN at work: enough data and the estimate will get there.

title: A/B Testing a Call to Action
text:
Bootstrap Standard Errors
A point estimate alone isn’t enough — we also want to know how precise it is. The bootstrap is a resampling method that estimates variability without requiring a closed-form formula. The idea: repeatedly resample (with replacement) from observed data, recompute the statistic each time, and use the standard deviation of those resampled statistics as the estimated standard error.

B = 1000
bootstrap_thetas = np.empty(B)

for i in range(B):
    resample_A = np.random.choice(draws_A, size=n, replace=True)
    resample_B = np.random.choice(draws_B, size=n, replace=True)
    bootstrap_thetas[i] = resample_A.mean() - resample_B.mean()

se_boot = bootstrap_thetas.std()

# Analytical SE for comparison
pi_A_hat = draws_A.mean()
pi_B_hat = draws_B.mean()
se_analytical = np.sqrt(
    pi_A_hat * (1 - pi_A_hat) / n + pi_B_hat * (1 - pi_B_hat) / n
)

ci_lower = theta_hat - 1.96 * se_boot
ci_upper = theta_hat + 1.96 * se_boot

print(f"Bootstrap SE:   {se_boot:.5f}")
print(f"Analytical SE:  {se_analytical:.5f}")
print(f"95% CI:         ({ci_lower:.4f}, {ci_upper:.4f})")

The two standard errors are nearly identical — reassuring confirmation that the bootstrap is working correctly. The 95% confidence interval runs from roughly 0.005 to 0.079. Since it excludes zero, it suggests CTA A likely outperforms CTA B, though the effect is small.

title: A/B Testing a Call to Action
text:
The Central Limit Theorem
The Central Limit Theorem (CLT) states that regardless of the underlying population distribution, the sampling distribution of the sample mean becomes approximately Normal as sample size grows. This applies to our estimator \(\hat{\theta} = \bar{X}_A - \bar{X}_B\) as well.
To visualize this, I simulate 1,000 values of \(\hat{\theta}\) at each of four sample sizes — \(n \in \{25, 50, 100, 500\}\) — and plot histograms.









At \(n = 25\), the histogram is rough and slightly lopsided. By \(n = 100\), it’s clearly bell-shaped, and by \(n = 500\) it’s nearly indistinguishable from a Normal curve (shown as the dashed overlay). The dotted vertical line marks the true \(\theta = 0.04\). This is the CLT in action: the shape of the underlying Bernoulli distribution stops mattering as the sample grows.

title: A/B Testing a Call to Action
text:
Hypothesis Testing
Now that we know \(\hat{\theta}\) is approximately Normal for large samples, we can use this to run a formal hypothesis test.
We set up:

\(H_0: \theta = 0\) — the two CTAs produce the same sign-up rate
\(H_1: \theta \neq 0\) — they differ

Under \(H_0\), the CLT tells us \(\hat{\theta}\) is approximately \(N(0, SE(\hat{\theta})^2)\). Standardizing gives us the test statistic:
\[z = \frac{\hat{\theta} - 0}{SE(\hat{\theta})}\]
By the CLT, \(z \overset{\cdot}{\sim} N(0,1)\) under \(H_0\) — so we know the distribution of our test statistic under the null, which is exactly what we need to compute a p-value.
A note on “t-test” vs. z-test: This setup is sometimes called a t-test, but that’s a loose use of the term. A classical t-test assumes Normal data and exact t-distributed test statistics. Our data are Bernoulli, not Normal, so there’s no exact t-distribution result here. The CLT gives us approximate Normality, and since we’re estimating the SE from data, what we’re really running is closer to a z-test. For large samples, the t and Normal distributions are nearly identical — so the distinction has little practical consequence, but it’s worth understanding why.

se = np.sqrt(
    pi_A_hat * (1 - pi_A_hat) / n + pi_B_hat * (1 - pi_B_hat) / n
)
z_stat = theta_hat / se

from scipy.stats import norm
p_value = 2 * (1 - norm.cdf(abs(z_stat)))

print(f"z-statistic: {z_stat:.3f}")
print(f"p-value:     {p_value:.4f}")

With a p-value of roughly 0.023 — below the conventional \(\alpha = 0.05\) threshold — we reject \(H_0\). The data provide statistically significant evidence that the two CTAs differ in sign-up rate, with CTA A performing better.

title: A/B Testing a Call to Action
text:
The T-Test as a Regression
The two-sample test above is mathematically equivalent to a simple linear regression. This is a useful connection because the regression framework generalizes naturally to more complex designs — adding control variables, interactions, or multiple treatment arms — while producing the same inference in the simple case.
We stack the data into a single dataset with outcome \(Y_i\) (1 = signed up, 0 = didn’t) and treatment indicator \(D_i\) (1 = saw CTA A, 0 = saw CTA B), then fit:
\[Y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 D_i + \varepsilon_i\]
The coefficient \(\beta_0\) is the mean of the B group (\(\hat{\pi}_B\)), and \(\beta_0 + \beta_1\) is the mean of the A group (\(\hat{\pi}_A\)). So \(\beta_1 = \pi_A - \pi_B = \theta\) — the OLS estimate \(\hat{\beta}_1\) is numerically identical to \(\hat{\theta}\).

import statsmodels.api as sm

Y = np.concatenate([draws_A, draws_B])
D = np.concatenate([np.ones(n), np.zeros(n)])
X = sm.add_constant(D)

model = sm.OLS(Y, X).fit()

title: A/B Testing a Call to Action
text:
The Problem with Peeking
Suppose your boss is impatient. Rather than waiting for all 1,000 visitors per group, she wants to check the results after every 100 visitors and stop early if a test comes back significant at \(\alpha = 0.05\).
This is a problem. A single test at \(\alpha = 0.05\) has a 5% false positive rate — 5% chance of rejecting \(H_0\) when it’s actually true. But each additional peek is another opportunity to get a false positive. Running 10 tests on accumulating data inflates the overall false positive rate well above 5%.
To quantify this, I simulate a world where the null is actually true (\(\pi_A = \pi_B = 0.20\), so \(\theta = 0\)), and measure how often the peeking strategy incorrectly rejects \(H_0\).

from scipy.stats import norm

def run_peeking_experiment(pi_A=0.20, pi_B=0.20, n_max=1000, step=100):
    draws_A = np.random.binomial(1, pi_A, n_max)
    draws_B = np.random.binomial(1, pi_B, n_max)
    for n in range(step, n_max + 1, step):
        xA, xB = draws_A[:n].mean(), draws_B[:n].mean()
        se = np.sqrt(xA*(1-xA)/n + xB*(1-xB)/n)
        if se == 0:
            continue
        z = (xA - xB) / se
        p = 2 * (1 - norm.cdf(abs(z)))
        if p < 0.05:
            return True  # At least one false positive
    return False

np.random.seed(0)
n_experiments = 10_000
false_positives = sum(run_peeking_experiment() for _ in range(n_experiments))
fpr_peeking = false_positives / n_experiments

print(f"False positive rate (peeking): {fpr_peeking:.3f}")
print(f"Nominal rate (single test):    0.050")

Nominal rate (single test):    0.050

The empirical false positive rate under peeking is roughly 18–22% — several times the nominal 5%. Every early look is another roll of the dice. In practice, this means A/B tests with peeking will regularly declare winners that don’t actually exist. The fix is to either pre-commit to a single test at a fixed sample size, use sequential testing methods designed for early stopping (like alpha-spending functions), or apply a Bonferroni correction across the planned number of peeks.

title: Replication of Card and Krueger (1994)
text:
Does raising the minimum wage kill jobs? For decades, the standard answer in economics was yes – basic supply-and-demand logic predicts that a binding price floor on labor should reduce employment. Card and Krueger (1994) challenged that consensus head-on.
Their setup was clean: on April 1, 1992, New Jersey raised its minimum wage from $4.25 to $5.05 per hour. Pennsylvania, right next door, left its minimum wage unchanged. Card and Krueger surveyed fast-food restaurants in both states before and after the increase, then compared employment trends across the “treatment” state (NJ) and the “control” state (PA).
The key insight is that New Jersey and Pennsylvania share a border, similar labor markets, and similar fast-food industries. Any aggregate shocks – a recession, a regional slowdown – should affect both states roughly equally. That makes Pennsylvania a credible counterfactual: what would have happened to NJ employment if the wage hadn’t gone up?
This is a difference-in-differences design. Instead of comparing NJ before vs. after (which conflates the wage increase with any other time trend), or NJ vs. PA at a single point in time (which conflates the wage effect with any pre-existing differences), DiD takes the difference of differences:
\[
\hat{\tau}_{DiD} = (\bar{Y}_{NJ,\text{after}} - \bar{Y}_{NJ,\text{before}}) - (\bar{Y}_{PA,\text{after}} - \bar{Y}_{PA,\text{before}})
\]
The parallel trends assumption – that NJ and PA employment would have moved together absent the policy – is what licenses a causal interpretation. It’s not testable directly, but the geography and industry focus make it more plausible than most natural experiments.
What did they find? Employment in New Jersey increased relative to Pennsylvania after the minimum wage hike. The result was surprising, influential, and controversial enough to help reshape how economists think about labor markets.
Below, I replicate Table 2 (summary statistics), Table 3 (the core DiD estimate), and Table 4 column i (OLS regression). As a bonus, I visualize the parallel trends logic directly – something the paper presents only in tabular form.

title: Replication of Card and Krueger (1994)
text:
Visualizing Parallel Trends
Card and Krueger present their results entirely in tables. The DiD logic is more intuitive visually. Below I plot average FTE employment in NJ and PA across both waves, alongside a counterfactual for NJ – what employment would have looked like had NJ followed PA’s trend instead of getting the wage increase.









The dashed line is the counterfactual: NJ employment declining slightly, in line with PA. Instead, NJ rose. The gap between the solid and dashed pink lines is the DiD estimate – roughly 2.75 FTE workers per store attributable to the minimum wage increase.
The parallel trends assumption is exactly that – an assumption. We can’t prove NJ would have followed PA’s path absent the policy. But the logic is defensible: the two states are adjacent, the fast-food industry was similarly structured in both, and Card and Krueger surveyed the same restaurants before and after, minimizing compositional noise.

title: Replication of Card and Krueger (1994)
text:
Takeaways
The replication holds up. The three core numbers from Table 3 – PA change ≈ -2.28, NJ change ≈ 0.47, DiD ≈ 2.75 – are consistent with the published paper, and the OLS regression in Table 4 confirms the same estimate with a standard error around 1.2.
What makes this paper’s design credible as a causal claim:

Natural experiment: NJ raised its minimum wage; PA didn’t. Card and Krueger didn’t have to randomize anything.
DiD structure: Differencing out time trends and pre-existing state differences isolates the policy effect, under the parallel trends assumption.
Within-industry comparison: Focusing on fast food reduces noise from industry mix. Both states had similar chains, similar ownership structures, and similar customer bases.

The finding challenged the textbook model of competitive labor markets and kicked off a large literature on minimum wages, monopsony, and labor market imperfections. The methodology – using geographic policy variation as a natural experiment – became a template for empirical work in economics throughout the 1990s and beyond.
